literal: Su Ancestor though merit reached the cosmos, still once offered tribute and called himself subject.
idiomatic: Su Ancestor's merit spanned the cosmos, yet he had once offered tribute and called himself a subject.

literal: Empress Mu bearing virtue of Kun the earth, again will be paired to enjoy the Qian position.
idiomatic: Empress Mu embodied earth's virtue and was again to be paired with heaven in sacrifice.

literal: This is ruler and subject sharing one mat, elder brother's wife and younger brother's husband in one chamber — scanning tomb records through the ages, there has not been this matter.
idiomatic: That would seat ruler and subject at one table and brother's wife with husband's brother in one hall — in all the tombs and annals, nothing like it exists.

literal: At the time Emperor Zhuangang's intent was sharp, court ministers dared not speak — only Yu and Personnel Minister Li Shenjun both had memorials heard.
idiomatic: Zhuangang's mind was set; no minister dared speak — only Yu and Personnel Minister Li Shenjun submitted memorials.

literal: Edict reply said: "Cultured and Solemn Emperor's merit reached the four quarters, the Way surpassed the hundred kings, therefore we examine and follow the old pattern, respectfully raising the honored title.
idiomatic: The edict answered: "Cultured and Solemn Emperor's merit reached the four seas and his Way surpassed the hundred kings; we therefore follow old precedent and raise his honored title.

literal: The prince's memorial says Han set the Grand Supreme at Xiang Street, Nandun at Chunling.
idiomatic: Your memorial cites Han's Grand Supreme at Xiang Street and Nandun at Chunling.

literal: Han Gaozu did not rely on melon-and-vine succession, Guangwu also had no virtue of generation upon generation — both personally received the mandate, not through fathers and grandfathers.
idiomatic: Han Gaozu did not inherit through collateral lines; Guangwu had no hereditary merit — both received the mandate themselves, not from forefathers.

literal: Separate temples and different shrines — in principle what difference?
idiomatic: Separate temples and different shrines — what difference in principle?

literal: Cultured and Solemn Emperor heaven's favor human dwelling, the sequence had its return.
idiomatic: Cultured and Solemn Emperor had heaven's favor and the people's dwelling; the succession had its due return.

literal: We humbly inherit the lower martial, thereupon master the divine vessel.
idiomatic: We humbly inherit the martial line and now hold the imperial throne.

literal: Since the imperial enterprise has its succession, Han's house is not the parallel.
idiomatic: Since the imperial line is continuous, the Han cases are not parallel.

literal: If by past measuring present, one should not move the shrine.
idiomatic: If the past governs the present, you say we should not move the shrine.

literal: Then Wei Taizu and Jin Jingdi though kingly traces were already manifest, both ended as human subjects — how can they share separate temples with the rest of emperors, lacking in the remaining order?
idiomatic: Yet Wei Taizu and Jin Jingdi, though their kingship was plain, died as subjects — can they have separate temples apart from other emperors and break the sequence?

literal: Han commanderies and states establishing temples — desired to honor Gaozu's virtue, making offerings reach all under heaven" not concerning Ancestral Temple spirit tablets, alone in outer shrines offering.
idiomatic: When Han commanderies and kingdoms built temples, it was to spread Gaozu's virtue through offerings everywhere — not the Ancestral Temple tablets kept in outer shrines.

literal: Han Xuan's father also was not from merit and virtue issuing forth — though not pursued in honor, is it not acceptable?
idiomatic: Xuandi's father likewise owed nothing to merit — though not ennobled posthumously, is that not acceptable?

literal: Father's younger brother's name is itself a title of honor and baseness — why must one follow antiquity and speak of non-kind?
idiomatic: The title father's younger brother is itself a rank of seniority — why must antiquity forbid what fits?

literal: Again saying ruler and subject in the same row, elder brother's wife and younger brother's husband sharing a chamber.
idiomatic: You also object that ruler and subject would sit in one row and brother's wife with husband's brother in one chamber.

literal: It should be because Cultured and Solemn Emperor in the past followed the subject's way — for this there is doubt.
idiomatic: That is because Cultured and Solemn Emperor once stood in the subject's place — hence your doubt.

literal: The Rites 'the Son of Heaven's eldest son is still like a scholar' — di and fu sacrifices, how can they not share one chamber?
idiomatic: The Rites say the crown prince is still like a scholar — for di and fu sacrifices, may they not share one hall?

literal: Moreover Jin Wen and Jing together are one generation — debaters say the world limit is seven, the main without fixed number.
idiomatic: Jin Wen and Jing belong to one generation; some say the limit is seven generations, but the main line has no fixed count.

literal: Zhao and Mu being the same, clearly there is principle of sharing a chamber.
idiomatic: If zhao and mu align, they clearly may share a chamber.

literal: Rites already have fu — elder brother's wife and younger brother's husband, what scruple?
idiomatic: The Rites already allow fu pairing — what scruple remains for brother's wife and husband's brother?

literal: The Rites, Great Ancestor and Father Ancestor one temple — how can there be no wife's uncle sharing a chamber?
idiomatic: Great Ancestor and Father Ancestor share one temple in the Rites — may wife's uncle not share a hall?

literal: If solely taking sharing a chamber as doubt, perhaps one may again deliberate moving and destroying.
idiomatic: If sharing a chamber alone is the objection, we may debate removal instead.

literal: Emperor Zhuangang already pressed by the younger sisters' request, this wording Yellow Gate Attendant Chang Jing and Secretariat Attendant Xing Zicai both approved.
idiomatic: Zhuangang, pressed by his younger sisters' plea, adopted language that Yellow Gate Attendant Chang Jing and Secretariat Attendant Xing Zicai had endorsed.

literal: Again posthumously honoring elder brother Prince of Pengcheng as Filial and Solemn Emperor.
idiomatic: He also posthumously honored his elder brother Prince of Pengcheng as Filial and Solemn Emperor.

literal: Yu again remonstrated to his face, saying: "Your Majesty acts without following law — how will posterity view it?
idiomatic: Yu remonstrated again in person: "Your Majesty acts without precedent — what will posterity see?

literal: Searching through books and records, there has not been this matter."
idiomatic: Search the books — nothing like this exists."

literal: The emperor did not follow.
idiomatic: The emperor would not listen.

literal: When the spirit tablets entered the temple.
idiomatic: When the tablets entered the temple,

literal: Again ordered all officials to accompany, entirely following the imperial carriage's form.
idiomatic: he again ordered every official to attend, all in the form reserved for the imperial carriage.

literal: Yu submitted a memorial considering: "From middle antiquity down to lower leaves, honoring ruler and kin, praising and clarifying merit and virtue — there were imperial titles, ultimately no emperor names.
idiomatic: Yu memorialized: "From middle antiquity to later ages, honoring rulers and kin and praising merit used imperial titles, never emperor names.

literal: Now if one removes emperor, leaving only imperial name, seeking it in ancient meaning, few have reliance.
idiomatic: To drop emperor and keep only imperial title finds little support in antiquity."

literal: Again not accepted.
idiomatic: Again the court did not accept it.

literal: When Erzhu Rong died, Yu was removed to Minister of Works.
idiomatic: After Erzhu Rong's death, Yu was made Minister of Works.

literal: When Erzhu Zhao led the host suddenly arriving, exiting the eastern side gate, he was seized by bandits.
idiomatic: When Erzhu Zhao's army suddenly arrived, Yu left by the eastern side gate and was seized.

literal: Seeing Zhao, his words and color did not bend; he was beaten by the Hu mob and died.
idiomatic: Before Zhao his speech and bearing did not break; the Hu mob beat him to death.

literal: At the end of Emperor Xiaowu he was posthumously given Grand General, Grand Preceptor, Grand Commandant, Recorder of the Secretariat affairs, posthumous title Cultured and Solemn.
idiomatic: At the end of Emperor Xiaowu's reign he was posthumously made Grand General, Grand Preceptor, Grand Commandant, and Recorder of the Secretariat, with the posthumous name Cultured and Solemn.

literal: Yu had beautiful bearing and wind, skilled in advancing and stopping — below cap and gown he had elegant rules of appearance.
idiomatic: Yu had fine presence and grace in movement; even in ordinary dress he kept an elegant bearing.

literal: Broadly reading the many books, not making chapter-and-sentence commentary; the literary pieces he composed, though many are lost, still have some transmitted in the world.
idiomatic: He read widely without pedantic glossing; much of his writing is lost, but some still circulates.

literal: Yet in office he could not be pure and white; what he advanced stopped at affinal kin — those with insight ridiculed him for it.
idiomatic: Yet in office he was not clean-handed; his promotions favored in-laws, which the knowing mocked.

literal: Without sons.
idiomatic: He had no sons.

literal: Younger brother Xiaoyou, in youth had reputation of the time, succeeded to Linhuai kingship, promoted in stages to Governor of Cangzhou.
idiomatic: His younger brother Xiaoyou, famed in youth, inherited Linhuai and rose to Governor of Cangzhou.

literal: In government warm and mild, liking to practice small favors, could not be pure and white yet without encroachment — the common people also for this found it convenient.
idiomatic: His rule was mild and fond of small favors; he was not clean but did not prey on the people, who found him easy to live under.

literal: Emperor Jing of Wei banqueted Qi Wenxiang at Hualin Garden; Xiaoyou because of drunkenness praised himself, also saying: "Your Majesty promised to grant me ability."
idiomatic: Emperor Jing of Wei feasted Qi Wenxiang at Hualin Garden; Xiaoyou, drunk, boasted and said, "Your Majesty promised to grant me talent."

literal: The emperor laughed and said: "We constantly hear the prince call himself pure."
idiomatic: The emperor laughed: "We always hear you call yourself incorrupt."

literal: Wenxiang said: "Prince of Linhuai in refined intent forgives offense."
idiomatic: Wenxiang said, "Prince of Linhuai in his refinement pardons the slip."

literal: Thereupon ruler and ministers all laughed and did not punish.
idiomatic: Ruler and ministers laughed and let it pass.

literal: Xiaoyou was clear in government principle, once submitted a memorial saying:
idiomatic: Xiaoyou understood governance and once submitted a memorial:

literal: Present regulations make a hundred households a party-clan, twenty households a lane, five households a neighboring unit.
idiomatic: "Present law makes a hundred households a party, twenty a lane, five a neighborhood.

literal: Within a hundred households there are twenty-five leaders; levies and labor are all exempt for them — bitter and sweet not equal.
idiomatic: Within each hundred households are twenty-five leaders exempt from levy and corvée — the burden falls unevenly.

literal: Sheep few, wolves many, again there is silkworm-devouring.
idiomatic: Too few bear the load, too many feed on it; layer on layer they devour the people.

literal: This as harm has been long.
idiomatic: This abuse is old.

literal: Capital wards — some seven or eight hundred households with only one lane chief and two clerks, miscellaneous affairs without lack — how much more the outer provinces?
idiomatic: In the capital some wards have seven or eight hundred households yet only one lane chief and two clerks, and affairs still run — how much more in the provinces?

literal: Request according to old establishment, the three chiefs' names not changed, yet a hundred households as unit, four lanes, two neighborhoods per lane — calculating clans, twelve fewer ding, obtaining twelve bolts of silk tribute.
idiomatic: Restore the old structure, keep the three chief titles, but make a hundred households the unit, four lanes, two neighborhoods per lane — twelve fewer adult males per clan, twelve bolts of silk tribute gained.

literal: Roughly calculating present registered households, should be more than twenty thousand clans — one year issuing twenty-four thousand bolts of silk tribute.
idiomatic: Roughly, registered households yield more than twenty thousand clans — twenty-four thousand bolts of silk a year.

literal: Fifteen ding produce one rotation soldier — calculating, obtaining sixteen thousand soldiers.
idiomatic: Fifteen ding supply one rotating soldier — about sixteen thousand troops.

literal: This is the way to enrich the state and settle the people.
idiomatic: That is the way to enrich the state and secure the people.

literal: Ancient feudal lords took nine women, scholars had one wife and two concubines.
idiomatic: Ancient feudal lords took nine wives; scholars had one wife and two concubines.

literal: Jin regulations: all princes set eight concubines;
idiomatic: Jin law allowed princes eight concubines;

literal: commandery lords and marquises, concubines six.
idiomatic: commandery lords and marquises six.

literal: Office Rank regulations: first and second rank have four concubines;
idiomatic: Office Rank law gave first and second ranks four concubines;

literal: third and fourth have three concubines;
idiomatic: third and fourth ranks three;

literal: fifth and sixth have two concubines;
idiomatic: fifth and sixth two;

literal: seventh and eighth have one concubine.
idiomatic: seventh and eighth one.

literal: Therefore yin teaching is grandly cultivated, continuing sacrifice has breadth.
idiomatic: Thus the women's quarter was maintained and the sacrificial line broadened.

literal: Broadening continuing heirs is filial piety.
idiomatic: Many heirs are filial piety.

literal: Cultivating yin teaching is ritual.
idiomatic: Maintaining the women's quarter is ritual.

literal: Yet the holy court suddenly abandoned these numbers — from coming it has been gradual and long; generals and ministers mostly esteem princesses, kings and marquises marry empresses' kin, therefore without concubine attendants, habit becomes constant.
idiomatic: Yet the court has long abandoned these numbers; ministers marry imperial princesses, kings and marquises take empresses' kin — concubines vanished and custom froze.

literal: Women mostly fortunate, born meeting this age — the whole court roughly without concubines, all under heaven nearly all one wife.
idiomatic: Women are fortunate to live now: the court almost has no concubines; the realm is nearly all monogamous.

literal: Suppose one forced will and broadly took wives — then family way scattered, personal affairs obstructed, inner and outer kin together would mock.
idiomatic: If a man forced himself to take many wives, his household would fracture, his affairs stall, and kin and neighbors would laugh.

literal: All people today universally lack standard and measure.
idiomatic: Today everyone lacks a standard.

literal: Parents marrying daughters then teach them jealousy;
idiomatic: Parents marrying daughters teach jealousy;

literal: aunts and elder sisters in meeting and sending off must mutually urge scruple.
idiomatic: aunts and sisters urge suspicion.

literal: Holding control of the husband as wife's virtue, taking ability at jealousy as woman's work.
idiomatic: Controlling the husband is called wifely virtue; skill in jealousy, woman's craft.

literal: Self-saying receiving people's bullying, fearing others' laughing at oneself.
idiomatic: They say they are bullied and fear being mocked.

literal: Kings and dukes still themselves one heart — how dare those below have two intents!
idiomatic: Even kings and dukes keep one heart — how dare inferiors have two!

literal: When jealousy's heart is born, then wife-and-concubine ritual is abolished;
idiomatic: When jealousy rises, wife-and-concubine ritual dies;

literal: wife-and-concubine ritual abolished, then adultery's omen rises — this is why your subject bitterly hates it.
idiomatic: when that ritual dies, adultery follows — this your subject bitterly hates.

literal: Request with kings and dukes, first rank taking eight, common wife to complete nine women;
idiomatic: Let kings, dukes, and first rank take eight concubines plus wife for nine women;

literal: according to office second rank completing seven;
idiomatic: second rank seven;

literal: third and fourth rank completing five;
idiomatic: third and fourth five;

literal: fifth and sixth rank then one wife two concubines.
idiomatic: fifth and sixth one wife and two concubines.

literal: Limit to one cycle, all ordered to fill the number.
idiomatic: Within one year all must fill their quota.

literal: If not filling the number, and awaiting concubines not by ritual, making the wife jealous and adding beating — remove the office held.
idiomatic: Whoever falls short, or keeps concubines irregularly, or lets a jealous wife beat them — strip his office.

literal: If the wife has no sons and does not take concubines, this is self-cutting-off — no way to blood-offer to grandfathers, request sentencing the unfilial crime, divorce and send away the wife.
idiomatic: A wife without sons who will not accept concubines cuts off the line — sentence unfilial conduct and divorce her.

literal: Your subject's red heart, righteousness solely for family and state, desires to make auspicious and inauspicious all not depart from ritual, noble and base each have their fit.
idiomatic: Your subject's sole aim is the family and state: let ritual govern fortune and misfortune, and each rank keep its place.

literal: Reduce people-leading to send out military ding, establish granaries to enrich grain food.
idiomatic: Cut petty chiefs to raise soldiers; build granaries to fill them.

literal: Set reward grids to capture treachery and theft, enact canonical orders to display court regulations.
idiomatic: Set rewards to catch thieves; publish statutes to show the court's law.

literal: May it make sufficient food and sufficient soldiers, people trust it.
idiomatic: Then food and arms will suffice and the people will trust the throne.

literal: Again presumptuously declaring wives' and concubines' numbers — just desires to make kings, marquises, generals, ministers, meritorious ministers' sons and younger brothers, seed and lineage fill the court, transmission without end — this is your subject's aspiration.
idiomatic: I also urge restoring concubine quotas so princes, ministers, and their sons may fill the court with heirs and the line never end — that is my wish."

literal: Edict handed to relevant offices, deliberation memorial different.
idiomatic: The edict went to the ministries; their report disagreed.

literal: Xiaoyou again said: "Now people alive as black slaves, burial imitating kings and marquises — alive and dead different paths, again without restraint.
idiomatic: Xiaoyou added: "Men live like bondsmen yet bury like princes — life and death follow different rules, and restraint is gone.

literal: Honoring and magnifying mound and ridge, flourishing ornament of sacrifice ritual — neighbors mutually glorify, calling it utmost filial piety.
idiomatic: They raise great mounds and lavish funerals; neighbors praise it as perfect filial piety.

literal: Also husband-and-wife's beginning is kingly transformation's first — sharing food and joining gourds suffices to complete ritual.
idiomatic: Marriage is the start of royal teaching; shared food and joined gourds are ritual enough.

literal: Yet today's rich increasingly extravagant, same-cage setting surpasses sacrificial trays.
idiomatic: Yet the rich grow more extravagant; wedding feasts outdo sacrificial spreads.

literal: Piling fish into mountains, mountains have forest trees, above forest trees phoenixes and simurghs exist.
idiomatic: They pile fish into mountains, set trees on them, and perch phoenixes atop —

literal: Only having troublesome labor, ultimately becoming abandoned cast-off — looking up to heaven's intent, perhaps it is not so.
idiomatic: mere labor ending in waste. Heaven's intent, I think, is otherwise.

literal: Request from now after, if marriage and burial exceed ritual, treat by violating the edict.
idiomatic: Henceforth, whoever exceeds ritual in marriage or burial violates the edict.

literal: If officials do not add investigation and impeachment, then same crime.
idiomatic: Officials who fail to investigate share the guilt."
